# Micah 5: Verse-by-Verse Research Notes

**How to use these notes:** Each point names its source page. One caution: many of the older commentaries (Barnes, Gill, Calvin, Clarke, Keil & Delitzsch, Wesley, Pulpit and others) came from the combined pages on biblehub.com and studylight.org. I read short extracts from those pages, not each full commentary.

---

**v. 1: The siege and the struck judge**
- **Plain meaning:** Guzik says Israel will be humbled by foreign powers, and even her judges will be insulted.  (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-5/)
- **The Hebrew numbering is different:** In the Hebrew Bible this verse closes chapter 4. Ellicott thinks it fits better there, and he says the striking of the judge was fulfilled in what happened to King Zedekiah.  (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/micah/5.htm)
- **"Mobilize your troops" or "slash yourself"?** The Hebrew verb usually means to cut oneself in grief. The NET, HCSB and Allen translate it that way, while the NASB and ESV translate it "muster." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/micah_5_commentary)
- **Whose siege is it?** Some take it as Sennacherib's in 701 BC (Allen, ESV Study Bible, Boice). Others take it as Nebuchadnezzar's (Kaiser, Barker, Wiersbe). Gill allows either Babylon or Rome. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/micah_5_commentary)
- **Is the struck judge Christ?** Gaebelein and Henry Morris say the judge is Jesus, slapped at His trial. Precept Austin disagrees, because Jerusalem was not under siege when Jesus was struck. Most writers say the judge is Zedekiah, though the scene can still foreshadow Christ. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/micah_5_commentary)
- **Matthew Henry (Presbyterian):** The judges had been corrupt and took bribes (3:11), so this disgrace was deserved, though it was still a disaster for Israel.  (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mic/Mic_005.cfm)

**v. 2: The ruler from Bethlehem**
- **Bethlehem's smallness:** Bethlehem was David's hometown but never an important city, yet God chose it for the Messiah's birth. The chief priests quoted this verse to Herod (Matthew 2:5–6).  (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-5/)
- **"Clans":** Ellicott explains "thousands" as a division of the tribes. He says Matthew's wording is a paraphrase that brings out the prophet's final meaning.  (https://biblehub.com/micah/5-2.htm)
- **Micah says "small," Matthew says "by no means least":** Keil & Delitzsch say this is not a contradiction. Matthew is pointing to the honour Bethlehem would gain from the Messiah's birth.  (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/micah/5-2.htm) Barnes makes a similar point: Micah describes Bethlehem as people saw it, while the priests in Matthew speak of it as God saw it.  (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/micah/5-2.html)
- **The names:** Spurgeon (Baptist) says "Bethlehem" means both "house of bread" and "house of war."  He takes Ephratah to mean "fruitfulness" or "abundance."  (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/micah/5-2.html)
- **"Origins of old" and the eternal Son:**
  - Guzik says Jesus came from Bethlehem but did not begin there.  (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-5/)
  - Ellicott links it to the creed: "Begotten of His Father before all worlds."  (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/micah/5.htm)
  - Matthew Henry, following Dr. Pocock, sees here Christ's eternal generation, a description that could fit no one else.  (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mic/Mic_005.cfm)
  - Kaiser and Fruchtenbaum say the Hebrew words for eternity here are the strongest available, and they are used of God in Psalm 90:2. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/micah_5_commentary)
- **Debate over "goings forth":** The Pulpit Commentary calls the word's meaning "somewhat doubtful." Many have read it as ancient promises and appearances of the Angel of the covenant, but Pulpit calls that "a forced interpretation."  (https://biblehub.com/micah/5-2.htm)
- **Response to Jewish readings:** Guzik rejects the view that the verse was fulfilled in David. Micah wrote long after David, so that reading gets the dates backwards.  (https://enduringword.com/blog-archive/qa-transcripts/can-women-be-deacons-was-phoebe-a-deacon-live-qa-with-pastor-david-guzik-april-19-2023-2/)
- **John Piper (Baptist):** God made sure Jesus was born in Bethlehem even though Mary and Joseph lived in Nazareth, because He was this ruler.  (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/from-little-bethlehem-will-come-a-ruler-in-israel)
- **A modern-scholarship caution:** Bob Utley (bible.org) quotes a reference work (NIDOTTE) saying the idea of an eternal, pre-existing Messiah does not appear in Jewish writings before the Similitudes of Enoch.  (https://bible.org/seriespage/micah-5)

**v. 3: Abandoned until she gives birth** *(the clearest split between traditions)*
- **Reformed:**
  - Calvin calls the Virgin Mary reading "a forced interpretation." He thinks the woman in labour is the whole people of God.  (https://www.ccel.org/c/calvin/comment3/comm_vol28/htm/iv.5.ii.htm)
  - Calvin's editor notes that most commentators disagree with Calvin and see Christ, born of a virgin, here.  (same URL)
  - The Geneva notes compare the Jews to women in labour who suffer a while before a happy delivery.  (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/micah/5-3.htm)
- **Catholic:** The Catholic Encyclopedia says the woman is Mary. It argues the woman cannot be Zion, because the surrounding words describe an individual, not a nation.  (https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/15464b.htm?vm=r) Catholic Answers suggests that Revelation 12's woman "with the pangs of birth" may point to this verse being fulfilled.  (https://www.catholic.com/qa/the-woman-in-revelation-and-the-pangs-of-childbirth)
- **The Virgin reading among Protestants:**
  - Barnes takes it as the Virgin who would bear Emmanuel.  (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/micah/5-3.html)
  - Ellicott (Anglican) says the nation would be brought very low "before the nativity of the Virgin-born."  (https://biblehub.com/micah/5-3.htm)
  - Pulpit notes that many say Zion, but it will not throw out the old Virgin reading.  (same URL)
  - Gill offers both: Mary, or the church bringing forth children to Christ. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/micah/5-3.html)
- **Wesleyan readers:**
  - Benson reads the woman as Zion freed from captivity, or better, the church bringing forth children of Jewish and Gentile birth. He expects a fuller fulfilment in Israel's conversion in the last days.  (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/micah/5-3.htm)
  - Adam Clarke says the woman is the Christian church of Revelation 12, until the full number of the Gentiles has come in.  (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/micah/5-3.html)
- **Pointing to a future for Israel:**
  - One commentary on the Biblehub page says "both may be meant." It argues the woman cannot be only Mary, since Israel is still "given up" long after Christ's birth.  (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/micah/5-3.htm)
  - Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel) sees the current Gentile age lasting until Israel "again begins to travail."  (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/micah/5-3.html)
  - Guzik says the verse was partly fulfilled in the Babylonian exile and will finally be fulfilled in the great tribulation.  (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-5/)
- **Early church:** Bible Hub's Q&A says early Christian writers such as Ignatius read the woman as Mary.  (https://biblehub.com/q/Micah_5_3_s_link_to_Messiah_s_Bethlehem_birth.htm)

**v. 4: The shepherd-king**
- Ellicott: the ruler joins a king's dignity with a shepherd's care. On "His God," Ellicott says the Messiah was to be subordinate to the Father ("My Father is greater than I").  (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/micah/5.htm)
- Matthew Henry: Christ fed "in the majesty of the name of the Lord" by teaching with His own authority, "Verily, verily, I say unto you."  (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mic/Mic_005.cfm)
- Guzik: His people stand secure because of His greatness.  (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-5/)

**v. 5: "He will be our peace" and the seven shepherds**
- **He is peace itself:** Guzik says He does not just bring peace, He is peace (Ephesians 2:14).  (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-5/) The NET note also points to Ephesians 2:14.  (https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=Mic&chapter=5&verse=5&theme=false)
- **Who is "the Assyrian"?**
  - *Matthew Henry:* the deliverance of Hezekiah from Sennacherib, which also pictures the church kept safe from Satan.  (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mic/Mic_005.cfm)
  - *Wesley:* "This man" is the Messiah. "We" means Hezekiah, the prophets and the people praying for deliverance.  (https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/micah-5.html)
  - *Ellicott:* Sennacherib's invasion does not fit the facts. He suggests the Maccabean period, or spiritually, Christian pastors.  (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/micah/5.htm)
  - *Keil & Delitzsch (Lutheran):* Asshur stands for the world's nations that attack the Lord's people.  (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/micah/5-5.html)
  - *Future-focused readers:* Wiersbe says this cannot be the Assyria of Micah's day. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/micah_5_commentary) A writer quoted on Precept Austin takes "the Assyrian" as the Antichrist of the last days.  (same URL) Chuck Smith goes further and calls it a last-days invasion by Russia.  (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/micah/5-5.html)
- **Seven shepherds, eight leaders:**
  - Most read "seven, even eight" as a set number standing for an open one: Wesley  and Matthew Henry. Henry applies the shepherds to magistrates and ministers.  (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mic/Mic_005.cfm)
  - The NET note says the numbers mean more than enough leaders.  (https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=Mic&chapter=5&verse=5&theme=false)
  - Keil calls them under-shepherds appointed by the Messiah.  (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/micah/5-5.htm)
  - Archbishop Newcome thought they were the Median and Babylonian leaders who took Nineveh.  (same URL)
  - Gill suggests New Testament writers, or the angels of Revelation 16.  (same URL)

**v. 6: Ruling Assyria and the land of Nimrod**
- Ellicott: "waste" literally means "feed upon," and the land of Nimrod stands for the world power opposed to God.  (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/micah/5.htm)
- Wesley: "they" are the seven shepherds and eight leaders, God's instruments to deliver His church.  (https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/micah-5.html)
- Utley: since Jewish soldiers never conquered Assyria, many take Assyria to mean any world power, defeated by the ideal ruler of vv. 2–5a.  (https://bible.org/seriespage/micah-5)

**v. 7: Like dew**
- Ellicott applies the verse to the returning exiles. He also sees it in the spread of the gospel through Jewish Christians scattered after Stephen's death.  (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/micah/5.htm)
- Matthew Henry: dew that "tarries not for man" shows God's people relying on God's grace rather than human help.  (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mic/Mic_005.cfm)
- Guzik: the deliverance will spread as wide as the dew.  (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-5/)
- Utley: some think the remnant is scattered Israel, others the end-time people of God.  (https://bible.org/seriespage/micah-5)

**v. 8: Like a lion**
- Ellicott: God shows righteous wrath as well as mercy. Christ is both the gentle Lamb and the Lion of Judah.  (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/micah/5.htm)
- Guzik places the full fulfilment in the millennium.  (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-5/)
- Utley allows that both pictures (dew and lion) may speak of judgment.  (https://bible.org/seriespage/micah-5)

**v. 10: Horses and chariots removed**
- Ellicott: the scene now moves to the church's purification. Horses were forbidden to Israel's kings (Deuteronomy 17:16), and they stand for human power, so the church will rely on God alone.  (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/micah/5.htm)
- Guzik: God removes things that are good in themselves (horses, cities) as well as evil things.  (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-5/)
- Utley: Israel was trusting in military power (v. 10), fortresses (v. 11), sorcery (v. 12) and idols (vv. 13–14).  (https://bible.org/seriespage/micah-5)

**v. 11: Cities and strongholds**
- Ellicott: walled cities will not be needed in the Messiah's kingdom (Micah 4:3).  (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/micah/5.htm)
- Precept Austin (future-focused): when the Messiah returns, Israel will trust only in Him.  (https://www.preceptaustin.org/micah_5_commentary)

**v. 12: Sorceries and fortune-tellers**
- Matthew Henry: God removes these because they are wicked, not only because they are useless. He compares Acts 19:19, where new believers burned their magic books.  (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mic/Mic_005.cfm)
- Bible Hub links verses 12–14 to Deuteronomy 18:10–12 and Exodus 20:4–5.  (https://biblehub.com/micah/5.htm)

**v. 13: Carved images and pillars**
- Bible Hub: this describes a return to pure worship and holiness.  (https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/micah/5.htm)
- Guzik: restored Zion will be allowed none of its old idolatries.  (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-5/)

**v. 14: Asherah poles**
- Ellicott: these were statues, pillars or trees used in the worship of Baal and Astarte. Manasseh put one in the temple and Josiah burned it (2 Kings 23:6). He reads "cities" as the corruption the cities protected.  (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/micah/5.htm)

**v. 15: Vengeance on the nations**
- **Translation:** Ellicott prefers "which have not been obedient" to the KJV's "such as they have not heard." In his view, these nations ignored their chances to learn the true faith.  (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/micah/5.htm)
- Guzik: in the millennium the nations too must live in purity before God.  (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-5/)
- Utley: God does not play favourites with nations, not even Israel and Judah.  (https://bible.org/seriespage/micah-5)

---

**The main split across the chapter.** In vv. 4–15, Matthew Henry, Wesley, Ellicott and Keil read the passage through Hezekiah's history, or as a picture of the church. Dispensational and futurist writers such as Guzik, Smith and Precept Austin's sources read it as Israel's restoration in the millennium. (Sources as cited above.)

**Not found:**
- Anything on v. 9 by itself.
- Orthodox (oca.org) readings.
- Anything from Pentecostal journals, Lutheran sites (lcms.org, 1517.org), bibleodyssey.org, or prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter.
- The NET notes on most verses. I only saw the v. 5 notes, plus the v. 1 translation as quoted on Precept Austin.

Further searches could fill these gaps.
